Destruction as gameplay and presentation

Authoritative destruction changes geometry, collision, cover, routes or structural state. Cosmetic VFX communicates those changes. A flipbook can depict dust/fire/impact but cannot by itself create a traversable breach, physical fragments or structural collapse.
Proposed event contract: event id and timestamp; world position and surface normal; material and damage phase; actual affected bounds; attack direction or impulse; gameplay importance; observer relationship; camera/distance context; chain/combo state; remaining cover and traversability state
Inference from multiple case studies, not any studio’s disclosed API. Gameplay code owns authoritative fields; VFX must not fabricate them.
Phase roles: anticipation or stress warning if gameplay provides one; contact/rupture at actual impact; directional primary mass displacement; secondary fragments and dust tied to material; clear reveal of changed space; residual visual aftermath with separate lifetime from collision
This is an explanatory role list, not a mandatory six-layer stack or fixed timing formula. Use only roles the event needs.
Can players locate the actual break and attack direction at normal play speed?
Can they correctly identify remaining cover and the newly available route?
Does the large mass move coherently before secondary noise dominates?
Does dust clear enough to support the next decision?
Do distant/low-quality versions preserve gameplay information?
Do simultaneous breaches remain distinguishable without exceeding measured target-device costs?

Reported production numbers

Into Spider-Verse studio page defines 24 images/s on ones and 12 on twos. Documented production description; no assertion the whole movie uses one cadence. [FM-S18]
Across maker interview explicitly includes animation on 1s, 2s, 3s through 6s, with variable/component-specific cadence. Documented industry practice. [FM-S19]
At a 24 fps film base, a hold of n frames lasts n/24 seconds: 1=41.7 ms, 2=83.3 ms, 3=125 ms, 4=166.7 ms, 5=208.3 ms, 6=250 ms. Arithmetic conversion, not recommended game hit-stop values; mentions 5 only as conversion, not evidence of a particular shot. [FM-S18, FM-S19]
Hi-Fi RUSH interview describes a 60 FPS target. Title-specific production target, not guaranteed performance or a general Roblox budget. [FM-S06]
Roblox tutorial currently prints dust Rate=50000. A source-quality warning, not adopted setting; engine caps, actual behavior and mobile costs require current specification/profiling. [FM-S33]

05 Juice and satisfaction table

The best-supported conclusion is conditional: feedback must preserve action and outcome information. More decoration is not a universal route to enjoyment or motivation. Experimental effect sizes refer to the tested builds and samples.

Success linked feedback rather than mere amplification

why it works (or fails): In the preregistered RPG experiment, outcomes mattered; occlusion is a proposed mechanism, not an isolated manipulation.
how to make it: Differentiate swing, hit and kill.
game uses: Combat, breaking, completion feedback
effect size if known: n=1,699. Success-dependence → competence +.45 [95% CI .30,.60]; effectance +.26 [.15,.36]; curiosity +.29 [.17,.41]. Unstandardised scale-point coefficients.
evidence level: study; JS01, A, 2024, Fig.4

Amplification can undermine experience

why it works (or fails): Tested non-success-dependent glow hid repeated impacts.
how to make it: Audit action–outcome legibility before increasing volume.
game uses: Rapid attacks
effect size if known: Amplification → effectance −.19 [−.36,−.03]; competence −.43 [−.68,−.19]. No significant direct enjoyment/playtime effect.
evidence level: study; JS01, A, 2024

Random variety is not established retention

why it works (or fails): Variability did not significantly predict curiosity or playtime.
how to make it: Use variation for appearance; test behavioural benefit.
game uses: Repeated pickups/hits
effect size if known: Enjoyment +.11 [.01,.22] scale points; curiosity −.01 [−.14,.11].
evidence level: study; JS01, A, 2024

An intermediate amount can beat extremes

why it works (or fails): One RPG bundled audiovisual changes, rather than isolating a particle setting.
how to make it: Compare complete builds; no transferable medium/high particle budget.
game uses: ARPG combat and menus
effect size if known: n=3,018. Partial η²: competence .005; autonomy .004; immersion .003; enjoyment .006; playtime .006; character level .006.
evidence level: study; JS02, A, 2020

Important qualification to the 2020 headline

why it works (or fails): None and Extreme both lost on playtime; enjoyment pairwise significance was Extreme < Medium/High, not None < Medium/High.
how to make it: Do not equate statistical significance with a large retention improvement.
game uses: Evaluation
effect size if known: Playtime F(3,3014)=5.83, p<.001; enjoyment F(3,3014)=5.87, p<.001. No numeric pairwise retention uplift found.
evidence level: study; JS02, A, 2020, §6

Impact feel features are candidates not proven causes

why it works (or fails): Review-derived game ranking plus descriptive feature inventory cannot isolate causes.
how to make it: Test hit-stop, sound coherence and camera control separately.
game uses: Fighting/beat-em-up
effect size if known: 281,720 Chinese reviews; 96 games, filtered to 44, then top/bottom 8 each. No causal effect size or feature correlation coefficient found.
evidence level: preprint; JS03, A, 2022; later IEEE GEM publication verified

Semantic text can clarify feedback

why it works (or fails): In a minimal targeting task, words communicated graded performance more clearly.
how to make it: Use readable success/outcome labels when needed; preserve meaning without particles.
game uses: UI, timing feedback, combat training
effect size if known: n=45; progress-feedback omnibus Kendall’s W=.44; means Text 5.62, Particles 4.43, None 2.81 (7-point scale).
evidence level: study; JS04, A, 2024, Table 2

Text plus particles is context dependent

why it works (or fails): No overall superiority of text over juicy particles; observation/performance stages showed no significant performance differences.
how to make it: Treat onomatopoeia as an optional style layer, not universal upgrade.
game uses: Comic effects, pickups
effect size if known: Study effects lasted 0.5 s; this is stimulus duration, not optimal lifetime.
evidence level: study; JS04, A, 2024, §§3.1,7–8

Fatigue contrast and audiovisual coherence

why it works (or fails): Interviewed audio designers reserve standout moments, vary repetition and align sounds with visible events.
how to make it: Keep frequent feedback restrained; let sound carry some impact.
game uses: Gunfire, footsteps, coin streams
effect size if known: 12 expert interviews; no causal effect size, optimal variant count or repetition threshold found.
evidence level: study (qualitative); JS05, A, 2024

Completion fitting and clean endings as design targets

why it works (or fails): Plausible perceptual/semantic goals; this search did not establish an effect-size recipe for them.
how to make it: Specify an unambiguous terminal state and test whether it reads as complete.
game uses: Coin counters, unlocks, assembly, UI success
effect size if known: no number found
evidence level: inference; requires validation

Repetition and the sound link

Keep semantic cues stable while varying decorative rotation, scale, secondary detail or selection. No universal variant count, random range, cooldown, combo step size or reset time is established. Test the actual cadence and multiplayer overlap. [inference; JS01, JS05]
Repetition can cause fatigue even when an isolated effect feels good. Aggregate low-priority decoration only if accepted inputs and outcomes remain clear. Combo escalation should communicate achieved state rather than add permanent intensity. [inference; JS01, JS05]
Use a shared event and an explicit visual landmark for sound alignment, then measure actual display and audio output on target devices. Broadcast and laboratory synchrony values below are not responsive-game latency budgets. [inference; AV01, AV02, JS05]

06 Mistakes table

Diagnosis should identify the moment and symptom, then name a concrete change and a retest. These fixes are hypotheses constrained by the cited principles, not automatic guarantees of a better effect.

Hitbox and visible area disagree

why it looks bad: The effect teaches an incorrect safe/unsafe boundary.
how to spot it: Overlay authoritative geometry through the full active interval.
fix: Correct the primary border before changing decoration; check every variant. [industry practice: ES-S01]

Every effect looks ultimate level

why it looks bad: Prominence stops predicting consequence.
how to spot it: Show ordinary/critical/ultimate events together and ask which matters.
fix: Reassign relative hierarchy; trim ordinary peaks rather than endlessly enlarging the ultimate. [inference from ES-S02]

Bright trail weak projectile head

why it looks bad: The eye follows decoration instead of collision.
how to spot it: Pause and identify the damaging part.
fix: Demote trail value/opacity/detail and clarify the head. [industry practice: ES-S04]

Too many unrelated shapes

why it looks bad: Meaning and motion direction become ambiguous.
how to spot it: Remove each layer individually and compare identification.
fix: Keep components with a specific role; replace conflicting silhouettes. [inference]

Uniform bright blob bloom wash

why it looks bad: Internal structure and nearby targets disappear.
how to spot it: Inspect normal and grayscale captures with bloom toggled.
fix: Reduce broad glow first; localize the peak and preserve dark/light structure. [inference]

Pretty in isolation invisible in play

why it looks bad: Preview background concealed a context problem.
how to spot it: Replay in actual maps/cameras with opponents and UI.
fix: Adjust contrast/shape or stage support, then retest; more saturation is not always sufficient. [industry practice: ES-S07, ES-S09]

Over detailed flipbook on phone

why it looks bad: The primary shape becomes shimmer or noise.
how to spot it: View at real projected size during movement.
fix: Select a coarser silhouette, shorten small debris tails or remove tertiary detail. [inference]

Linear timing everywhere

why it looks bad: Equal rates obscure acceleration and release.
how to spot it: Plot size/speed/value over time and inspect main transitions.
fix: Retune the dominant parameter first; preserve deliberately constant projectiles. [inference from ES-S07]

Extra swelling before an instant impact

why it looks bad: A response reads as late or soft.
how to spot it: Compare gameplay contact timestamp with the visible peak.
fix: Start at a suitable energetic flipbook frame or choose another asset; do not move the gameplay hit casually. [inference]

Every secondary layer peaks together

why it looks bad: Complexity collapses into one unreadable mass.
how to spot it: Solo the core and compare the combined first peak.
fix: Offset only secondary motion/dissipation while preserving contact alignment. [industry practice: ES-S09]

Lingering danger after damage ends

why it looks bad: The player may keep avoiding a harmless area.
how to spot it: Review the final active tick alongside the remaining visual.
fix: End the semantic hazard cue; retain only clearly different residue if useful. [inference]

Uniform opacity fade on an asset needing breakup

why it looks bad: The silhouette can look like a flat card being switched off.
how to spot it: Watch the tail against both light and dark surfaces.
fix: Select a breakup flipbook or size/shape tail; retain simple fades when they read better. [inference]

Randomization changes the gameplay message

why it looks bad: Variants imply different reach, intensity or direction.
how to spot it: Compare extremes of randomized settings.
fix: Randomize ornamental parameters inside tested bounds; lock semantic geometry and event timing. [inference]

Same colour means opposite actions

why it looks bad: Vocabulary loses reliability.
how to spot it: Ask new players to classify unknown examples.
fix: Define colour plus shape/motion roles and correct exceptions. [inference]

Camera motion masks next action

why it looks bad: Feedback consumes control or visibility.
how to spot it: Aim/navigate during the effect rather than watching a reel.
fix: Lower/remove the troublesome layer and offer reduced camera effects. [inference]

Late body hit effect appears on the head

why it looks bad: Correct simulation looks incorrect.
how to spot it: Frame-step a moving/crouching target with latency telemetry.
fix: Use body-part-specific confirmation/attachment only after testing occlusion trade-offs. [industry practice: ES-S18]

Expensive polish hides weak timing

why it looks bad: An impressive shader cannot clarify the event sequence.
how to spot it: Replace appearance with simple grayscale parts.
fix: Fix event shape/timing before restoring polish. [industry practice: ES-S10, ES-S09]

A laboratory number becomes an aesthetic default

why it looks bad: The task/display/population changed.
how to spot it: Inspect each numeric field’s source and context.
fix: Keep study outcomes in evidence fields; obtain game-specific test bounds. [inference]

Calling a small p value a large design gain

why it looks bad: Statistical significance does not give magnitude or external validity.
how to spot it: Check effect-size unit, confidence interval, game/sample and actual contrast.
fix: Report the numeric effect and scope; do not promise a retention percentage.

Calling random variation curiosity

why it looks bad: Unpredictability can be meaningless.
how to spot it: Player sees different colours but cannot learn anything useful.
fix: Keep variation decorative or connect it to interpretable gameplay state.

Randomising the contact frame

why it looks bad: Separates consequence from action.
how to spot it: Compare earliest visible contact with audio and gameplay event.
fix: Keep sync anchor fixed; vary tails/secondary details instead.

Treating 25 percent as a whole screen flashing allowance

why it looks bad: Wrong geometry for WCAG’s visual-field criterion.
how to spot it: Look for denominator and viewing-distance assumptions.
fix: Use visual-field analysis and correct standards-aware tooling.

A safety warning replacing a fix

why it looks bad: Exposure can precede a player’s ability to disable the effect.
how to spot it: Known failures still ship behind a splash screen.
fix: Redesign failure and validate the composite output.

All effects off removes warnings

why it looks bad: Lower decoration also deletes essential information.
how to spot it: Play reduced-effects mode without sound.
fix: Preserve or replace the semantic cue with a stable readable one.

Colour blind filter treated as proof

why it looks bad: People and contexts vary.
how to spot it: Only simulation has been checked.
fix: Use redundant signifiers, customization and actual player testing.

Authoring timestamps treated as output sync

why it looks bad: Display/audio pipelines add different delay.
how to spot it: Code says simultaneous but a capture shows separation.
fix: Measure emitted audio and displayed frames on target hardware.

Using emission cap as scene budget

why it looks bad: Often fails under overlapping effects and large transparent sprites
how to spot it: Count seems legal but on-device GPU frame time spikes
fix: Budget visible area/concurrency and measured CPU/GPU cost, preserving essential cue

Random starting a telegraph explosion

why it looks bad: Skips designed buildup or jumps straight into dissipation
how to spot it: Event begins on inconsistent visual states
fix: Disable random start for semantic one-shots; vary approved secondary elements instead

Treating additive as universal blending

why it looks bad: Smoke and volume disappear against bright backgrounds; overlap washes out hierarchy
how to spot it: Inspect against bright stage and grayscale
fix: Normal blending for obscuring mass; additive only for luminous portions

Doubling layers without distinct roles

why it looks bad: Muddies silhouette and increases overdraw
how to spot it: Solo/mute each layer and name what information changes
fix: Keep one primary read; remove redundant layers before adding detail

Increasing sheet frames without checking cell resolution

why it looks bad: More temporal detail can mean blurrier individual drawings
how to spot it: Inspect per-cell artwork size and close-up phone capture
fix: Choose fewer useful cells or a better-fitting aspect ratio; verify actual resident detail

Pooling without complete reset

why it looks bad: Teleport streaks, stale particles or persistent glow appear
how to spot it: Interrupt/reacquire rapidly and inspect the first new frame
fix: Clear history, reset properties and callbacks; respect outstanding lifetime/TimeScale

Relying on unsupported post effects

why it looks bad: Recipe cannot be implemented as written or substitution changes its meaning
how to spot it: Property/class absent from current public API
fix: Specify an honest approximation or request another approved asset; no invented API

Cheap or disconnected spectacle

why it looks bad: A large flourish can contradict a minor outcome or hide that nothing changed; this is a design diagnosis, not a measured universal law.
how to spot it: Compare the claimed importance with the actual state change; mute sound and remove tertiary layers.
fix: Rebuild the primary contact/state cue, then add only a layer with a distinct job. [inference]

Mushy or floaty impact

why it looks bad: Uniform speeds and diffuse edges can fail to show where force was transferred.
how to spot it: Scrub first contact and follow-through; check whether heavy pieces move like fine dust.
fix: Concentrate contact timing and separate mass motion from decorative tails; test the revised feel. [inference; ES-S09]

07 Roblox table

Current engine facts are Spec evidence, not proof of artistic quality. Living documentation was accessed on 13 October 2026. Defaults and limits can change, so verify the affected API before implementation.

ParticleEmitter emission

what it is good for: Bursts, ambient motes, sparks, smoke
key properties and values: Rate; Enabled; Lifetime; Emit(n); Clear()
limits and mobile cost: 400/s per emitter; mobile 100/s. Lifetime cap 20 s. Screen area and overlap matter.
best practice: Inference: explicit bursts for discrete impacts; choose count by measured cost and readability.
source: RB01; RB02

ParticleEmitter flipbook layout

what it is good for: Authored animated sprite sheets
key properties and values: None; 2×2/4×4/8×8; Custom via FlipbookSizeX/Y. Custom axes 1–64.
limits and mobile cost: Texture dimensions must divide by grid; padding reduces bleed; unique sheets cost memory.
best practice: Inference: record cell geometry and empty cells; reject incompatible assets.
source: RB01; RB03; RB36

ParticleEmitter playback

what it is good for: One-shot punch or looping motion
key properties and values: Loop, OneShot, PingPong, Random; fps ≤30; BlendFrames; StartRandom.
limits and mobile cost: OneShot ignores fps; low-memory clients can disable flipbooks.
best practice: Inference: retain authored first frame for important one-shots; blending off for held drawings.
source: RB01; RB02; RB04

ParticleEmitter appearance

what it is good for: Tint, opacity, glow, shaping
key properties and values: Color/Size/Transparency sequences; LightEmission 0 normal, 1 additive; LightInfluence 0–1; Brightness.
limits and mobile cost: Emission does not light the scene. Brightness applies with LightInfluence=0.
best practice: Inference: use separate local light only when world illumination adds needed information.
source: RB01

ParticleEmitter placement time

what it is good for: Flow, elongation, layering, local slow motion
key properties and values: Orientation; Rotation/RotSpeed; Squash; ZOffset; TimeScale 0–1.
limits and mobile cost: ZOffset changes render depth, not geometry. No native per-frame-duration list found.
best practice: Inference: use attachment transforms; record phase timing and cleanup explicitly.
source: RB01; RB02

Attachment

what it is good for: Shared origin and direction for effect layers
key properties and values: CFrame, WorldCFrame; local position/orientation; links Beam/Trail endpoints.
limits and mobile cost: Point emission differs from BasePart-volume emission. No safe instance count found.
best practice: Inference: anchor to contact normal/muzzle/foot socket rather than eyeballing world offsets.
source: RB07

Beam

what it is good for: Tethers, directional energy, arcs, continuous laser silhouettes
key properties and values: Attachment0/1; Width0/1; CurveSize0/1; Segments; FaceCamera; texture controls.
limits and mobile cost: Default Segments=10; at least n−1 for n keypoints. Overdraw still applies.
best practice: Inference: minimal segment count that retains silhouette and sequences; endpoints match gameplay.
source: RB05

Beam texture light

what it is good for: Scrolling streak detail and emissive appearance
key properties and values: TextureSpeed in cycles/s; Wrap/Static/Stretch; Brightness 0–10000, default 1.
limits and mobile cost: LightEmission does not illuminate geometry; high brightness is not a design recommendation.
best practice: Inference: use explicit units; recheck pattern speed after changing TextureLength/Mode.
source: RB05

Trail

what it is good for: Sword swings, moving projectiles and motion history
key properties and values: Attachment0/1; Lifetime 0.01–20 s (default 2); MinLength; MaxLength; WidthScale 0–1; Clear().
limits and mobile cost: MaxLength=0 removes distance cap. Quality levels affect trail fidelity.
best practice: Inference: clear pooled trail history before reuse/teleport; trim lifetime to avoid stale threat paths.
source: RB06; RB24

Highlight

what it is good for: Readable object/target silhouette or outline
key properties and values: Adornee; DepthMode AlwaysOnTop/Occluded; fill and outline colors/transparencies.
limits and mobile cost: 255 client slots; disabled instances occupy slots; excess ignored.
best practice: Inference: allocate by importance; destroy permanently retired highlights; avoid unintended through-wall information.
source: RB08

PointLight

what it is good for: Omnidirectional impact/torch illumination
key properties and values: Brightness, Color, Range, Shadows; direct BasePart/Attachment child.
limits and mobile cost: Range ≤120 studs. Shadow cost grows with affected geometry/light density.
best practice: Inference: choose shortest useful range; test shadowless version before adding shadows.
source: RB09; RB12; RB13; RB29

SpotLight

what it is good for: Directed muzzle/cone/flashlight illumination
key properties and values: Angle, Face, Range plus shared Light properties.
limits and mobile cost: Range ≤120 studs; geometry and shadows determine cost; no universal light-count budget found.
best practice: Inference: align with the actual action direction and keep gameplay visibility independent.
source: RB10; RB12; RB13

SurfaceLight

what it is good for: Illuminated panels and broad surface glow
key properties and values: Face, Angle, Range; behaves like SpotLight under Attachment.
limits and mobile cost: Range ≤120 studs. A luminous texture is not a substitute for world lighting.
best practice: Inference: prefer one purposeful source to overlapping redundant lights.
source: RB11; RB13

Lighting

what it is good for: Scene value/palette baseline and rendering intent
key properties and values: LightingStyle Soft/Realistic; PrioritizeLightingQuality; Ambient, ExposureCompensation.
limits and mobile cost: Technology is deprecated; quality priority trades shading against viewing distance.
best practice: Inference: approve the environment first; tune VFX on all shipped lighting profiles.
source: RB13; RB37

Atmosphere

what it is good for: Depth, haze and scene mood
key properties and values: Density, Offset, Color, Decay, Glare, Haze.
limits and mobile cost: Can obscure objects; poor Offset balance exposes ghosting or distant LOD popping. No universal safe density found.
best practice: Inference: test distant threats against haze; do not use fog to conceal critical telegraphs.
source: RB14

BloomEffect

what it is good for: Glow around bright features
key properties and values: Intensity; Size in pixels; Threshold 0 all colors, 1 pure white.
limits and mobile cost: May vary with quality; full-scene cost/readability interaction. No useful universal intensity number found.
best practice: Inference: preserve the primary silhouette with bloom disabled.
source: RB16; RB15

BlurEffect

what it is good for: Defocusing the world behind a menu
key properties and values: Size is Gaussian blur radius in pixels.
limits and mobile cost: Global 3D blur; not radial/motion blur. Quality-dependent.
best practice: Inference: avoid obscuring active danger during gameplay.
source: RB17; RB15

ColorCorrectionEffect

what it is good for: Mood tint and localized player feedback
key properties and values: Brightness −1 black/+1 white; Contrast; Saturation −1 grayscale; multiplicative TintColor.
limits and mobile cost: Post effects do not alter GuiObjects; additive brightness may erase value structure.
best practice: Inference: preserve HUD contrast separately and verify no-flash/reduced-effects variants.
source: RB18; RB15

DepthOfFieldEffect

what it is good for: Controlled reveal/shop focus
key properties and values: FocusDistance and InFocusRadius in studs; NearIntensity, FarIntensity.
limits and mobile cost: Quality-dependent; can hide foreground/background threats. No safe intensity range found.
best practice: Inference: reserve strong focus changes for moments without targeting demands.
source: RB19; RB15

SunRaysEffect

what it is good for: Sun-linked atmosphere
key properties and values: Intensity; Spread 0–1.
limits and mobile cost: Not a general local volumetric-light beam. Quality-dependent.
best practice: Inference: use Beam for designed local streaks, acknowledging that it is a different effect.
source: RB20; RB15

ColorGradingEffect

what it is good for: Global tone-mapper style
key properties and values: TonemapperPreset Default/Retro.
limits and mobile cost: Lighting-only; most recently parented instance wins.
best practice: Inference: do not treat it like stackable, camera-local color correction.
source: RB21; RB35

Camera

what it is good for: Scripted kick, shake and zoom
key properties and values: CurrentCamera.CFrame; FieldOfView 1–120°, default 70; CameraType; render-step scheduling.
limits and mobile cost: No named universal shake amplitude/duration found here. Defaults can fight manually assigned CFrame.
best practice: Inference: layer offset into camera controller, offer reduction/off, reset and unbind on cancellation.
source: RB22; RB23

Graphics quality

what it is good for: Adaptive visual fallback
key properties and values: Engine QualityLevel 1–21; saved player setting 1–10; Automatic.
limits and mobile cost: Platform-specific particle/trail/post-effect scaling. The two enums are not interchangeable.
best practice: Inference: test low, high and automatic on actual devices; essential information survives each.
source: RB24; RB25

Texture import and streaming

what it is good for: Correct, reusable sprite assets
key properties and values: PNG with alpha suits particles; general texture upload allowance up to 4096×4096; streaming varies detail.
limits and mobile cost: Current texture page has conflicting UV 1024 wording; particle effective 4K not established.
best practice: Inference: record source dimensions and tested runtime quality separately; reuse asset IDs.
source: RB26; RB27; RB32; RB02

Unsupported native controls in inspected API

what it is good for: Avoid unrealizable agent recipes
key properties and values: No dedicated chromatic-aberration, radial-blur, refraction/distortion post effect; no ParticleEmitter depth-fade or per-cell duration property found.
limits and mobile cost: This is an inspected-public-API finding, not proof that every approximation is impossible.
best practice: Inference: use authored overlays, separate stages, mesh silhouettes or approved existing assets; never relabel Gaussian blur as radial blur.
source: RB01; RB33

A practical kitbashing workflow


1 Choose for communication before decoration

Action: Identify what the event is, what it does and how strong it is. Find a primary sheet whose silhouette, direction and built-in phases already fit. An attractive explosion sheet is a bad warning indicator if its visible boundary or timing conflicts with gameplay. Numeric selection weights: no number found.
Evidence: industry practice + inference; RB38

2 Inspect the sheet as data and animation

Action: Preview all cells, contact sheet, first/peak/last frame, loop transition and animation against bright/dark backgrounds. Record whether the first frame is transparent, where peak energy occurs, whether it already contains sparks or smoke, and which cells are empty. Do not layer duplicate information merely because multiple assets exist.
Evidence: inference; RB01, RB03, RB04

3 Split roles across parts

Action: Use primary sprite shape for the main event; supplemental sparks for direction/material, mesh pieces for real depth/parallax, Beam for continuous path, Trail for motion history, light for surrounding-world response, and ground mark for remaining evidence. A number of layers that is universally rich-but-clear: no number found. Each layer needs a distinct job and a removable quality tier.
Evidence: industry practice + inference; RB38, RB39

4 Choose temporal mode deliberately

Action: OneShot for an authored beginning-to-end event. Loop only if the endpoints are compatible. PingPong suits reversible motion, not expanding explosions that would visibly run backward. Random is for interchangeable organic frames. Disable random start when onset carries gameplay meaning.
Evidence: spec + inference; RB01, RB04

5 Preserve drawn timing

Action: FlipbookBlendFrames=false retains abrupt drawing changes; true linearly crossfades and can soften/double silhouettes. For variable holds, use repeated cells in a preprocessed sheet or distinct timed phase assets. Roblox exposes no per-cell hold list in the inspected API. This agent should choose available cadence variants; repacking is a separate asset-processing step if authorized.
Evidence: spec + inference; RB01, RB04

6 Match texture tint and blending

Action: Neutral texture artwork is generally easier to tint predictably; multiplying tint cannot reconstruct detail missing from the source. Normal/alpha-like blending preserves dark smoke and silhouettes; additive blending suits luminous accents and brightens overlap. Check both against the actual scene. LightEmission is not world illumination. Use pre-authored soft alpha edges and placement to reduce intersections; a true exposed depth-fade control was not found.
Evidence: spec + inference; RB01, RB02

7 Integrate spatially

Action: Share a meaningful origin/axis across layers; align bursts with contact normal or action path. Compare camera-facing sprites from playable angles against real mesh depth. Place a small source cue at the emitter/contact point so the billboard appears caused by an action. ZOffset is only a rendering adjustment and must not falsify a warning footprint.
Evidence: inference; RB07, RB05, RB06

8 Hide repetition without changing meaning

Action: Vary allowed rotation, size, speed/lifetime, starting frame for loops and selected assets, using a saved seed for reproducible review. Do not randomize critical contact time, danger boundary, team meaning or power rank. Random UV mirroring is not a ParticleEmitter property in the inspected API; use available mirrored asset variants if they exist. Universal variant count, randomization percentage, cooldown, combo step or reset time: no number found.
Evidence: spec + inference; RB01, RB38

9 Make repetition cheaper

Action: For repeated footsteps/gunfire/coins, retain the event cue and reduce secondary trails, persistent smoke and camera response before the cue itself. Test maximum design concurrency and the user-requested 1000-repeat scenario. Throttle cosmetic events by a measured client budget; maintain a distinct allowance for critical signals. Choose limits from telemetry, not a purported platform-wide magic number.
Evidence: inference; RB29, RB30

10 Integrate sound and completion

Action: Place an explicit synchronization marker on the action/contact frame and on the sound transient; verify recorded playback together. Identify the final cell and cleanup state. Do not infer that a sheet beginning at frame zero has its impact on that first frame. No perceptual audiovisual timing tolerance was researched in this API-focused contribution.
Evidence: inference; RB38

Performance and mobile validation

A visual budget is a measured scene envelope on a target device, not a single particle count. No universal low-end-mobile total, VFX-only milliseconds, transparent coverage percentage, unique-sheet limit or safe dynamic-light count was found.
Evidence: spec + inference; RB02, RB24, RB28, RB29, RB30, RB31, RB34

cost model

GPU: projected transparent area, repeated overlap, shading/post effects and shadowing.
CPU: spawning, scripting, property churn, instance management and any real physics debris.
Memory/loading: unique textures/meshes, resident mips, pool retention, preload scope and asset duplication.
Networking: transmit authoritative event information; create presentation locally where appropriate. Client visuals never replace server gameplay authority.

optimization order

Preserve danger footprint, source/target identity and important onset.
Remove offscreen or irrelevant cosmetic layers, considering whether their lights still affect visible geometry.
Reduce broad overlapping smoke/glow and long low-information tails before shrinking the meaningful silhouette.
Reuse approved asset IDs; replace unnecessary unique sheets; test smaller textures/cell counts.
Simplify distant effects by projected readability and importance; avoid exact cut distances until measured.
Reduce real debris physics and shadows; choose cheaper non-colliding visual pieces when game rules permit.
Avoid unnecessary per-frame emitter property changes; bake stable properties into templates.
Pool only if profiling shows a benefit; bound pools, reset state and account for retained memory.
Reprofile the complete scene after each change; a removed CPU cost may expose a GPU bottleneck.

mobile test plan

Select a real low-end baseline from the intended audience; record model, OS, client build, resolution, quality and power/thermal state. Add actual iOS/Android targets as audience requires. Studio emulator checks layout, not real memory or thermal behavior.
Record representative scene without optional VFX, then the same deterministic event/camera route with the effect; distinguish CPU-bound from GPU-bound frames.
Test one event, normal gameplay, worst plausible gameplay concurrency and repeated retriggers using the game’s real spawn/cooldown rules. Include close-up billboard coverage, camera inside smoke and dense overlapping effects.
Test lowest/highest explicit quality and Automatic. Verify the same essential meaning if flipbooks/post effects reduce or disappear. Do not assume quality enum values map directly.
Exercise cold loading, reuse, cancelled effects, pooled reacquisition, respawn, teleport and streamed-in areas; inspect for missing onsets, ghosts, leak-like memory growth and lingering connections.
Perform 10–15 minutes of active mobile gameplay and compare late-session frame times/memory with initial runs, per Roblox hardware-test guidance.
Capture on-device MicroProfiler, Developer Console memory, frame-time distributions and crashes. Define project pass/fail thresholds before comparing variants; 60 FPS/16.67 ms is the documented total-frame target, not all for VFX.
After publication, compare device-class performance and crashes; keep visual-review evidence alongside telemetry. Fix regressions on the limiting device before raising cosmetic tiers.
Pooling caution: Pooling VFX is an inference/application of general reuse principles, not a measured guarantee from these docs. Reserve separate active instances for overlapping events. Reset Enabled, TimeScale, transforms, color, sequences, light state, connections and deadlines; clear old particle/trail history before reuse. Never clear an instance still playing another event. Highlight slots remain occupied by disabled pooled instances.

Derived arithmetic examples


Cell resolution

Calculation: 1024×1024 atlas / 8×8 grid = 128×128 pixels/cell; usable artwork is smaller when padding is included.
Context: Not a promise of runtime mip/resolution.
Evidence: inference (arithmetic); RB02, RB03

Uniform OneShot timing

Calculation: N meaningful or repeated cells across lifetime L: each cell occupies L/N seconds; nominal unique updates depend on repeated cells.
Context: Empty cells are still part of the timeline. No recommended explosion duration follows.
Evidence: inference (arithmetic); RB04

Hypothetical uncompressed RGBA8 memory

Calculation: 256²: 0.25 MiB; 512²: 1 MiB; 1024²: 4 MiB; 2048²: 16 MiB; 4096²: 64 MiB, before mips. Ideal full mip chain approximately multiplies by 4/3.
Context: Not measured Roblox GPU memory. Formats, compression, streaming and residency can differ.
Evidence: inference (arithmetic under declared assumptions); RB29

Expected continuous population

Calculation: For stable rate r and independent lifetime T, expected active particles ≈r×E[T] after reaching steady state, absent culling or other clamps. Add live particles from bursts.
Context: Not an engine budget, and not exact under throttling, TimeScale changes or clipping.
Evidence: inference (model); RB01

Frame count conversion

Calculation: Duration in ms = frame count × 1000 / reference fps. Derived examples at a 24 fps base: one frame 41.67 ms; a two-frame hold 83.33 ms; a six-frame hold 250 ms.
Context: Conversions explain timebases only. These are not recommended impact durations, and film exposure cadence is not engine simulation rate.
Evidence: inference (arithmetic); 

08 Effect card template

Start here before selecting assets or reviewing a finished effect. The card records facts, choices and evidence separately so a later designer can explain each change.

Communication job

Fill in: What is it? What does it do? How large or consequential is its actual impact? Name the gameplay state the player must understand.

Importance rating

Fill in: Record separate caster, ally and enemy ratings on the project’s chosen scale. Riot documents 1–10; no universal mapping to size, value, duration or count is established. Record why this cue outranks its neighbors.

Moment and intended feeling

Fill in: Name the event and intended feeling. Distinguish information that must be perceived from optional embellishment.

Authoritative trigger and truth

Fill in: Event source, position, direction, area/hitbox, activation and expiry, targetability, cancellation and prediction/reconciliation behavior. Decorative shape cannot silently change any of these.

Audience and visibility

Fill in: Caster, ally, enemy, spectator, distance, camera angle, occlusion rules and privacy of information. State which secondary layers each audience can omit.

Asset inventory

Fill in: Asset IDs and rights; flipbook grid, frame count, resolution per cell, intended rate, loop/one-shot mode, premultiplication/edge assumptions, and whether random start preserves meaning.

Primary shape and silhouette

Fill in: Identify the single dominant shape, focal point, direction, source and target. Record small-screen and grayscale checks.

Value and colour

Fill in: Dominant palette, accent, core/edge relationship, stage backgrounds, team/rarity/status redundancy. Use project measurements; no universal ratios established.

Layer roles

Fill in: List primary, secondary and tertiary layers with each layer’s communication purpose, emitter/beam/trail/part/light type, orientation, attachment, and stop condition. Remove roles duplicated without benefit.

Timing per phase

Fill in: Windup, punch, crescendo, follow-through and dissipation. Store durations in seconds or ms with their source and context; if frames, store the relevant fps/timebase. Unsupported values remain unset, not zero.

Motion and scale

Fill in: Start/end size, life curves, speed, acceleration, arcs, overlap, squash/stretch, rotation, inherited motion and world/camera alignment. State how they affect the intended feeling.

Sound link

Fill in: Named sound event, visual sync landmark, trigger timestamp, intended relative offset, source-supported tolerance if available, and measured latency on target device. Keep network arrival separate from asset timing.

Camera and screen response

Fill in: Shake/kick/zoom/flash/blur/slow motion: scope, affected player, optionality, accessibility controls and restoration behavior. Omit if it impairs the required task.

Repetition and escalation

Fill in: Allowed variants, semantic invariants, aggregation/cooldown/cap policy, combo escalation rule and reset condition. No count, delay or step size is a universal default.

Scene competition

Fill in: Worst-case simultaneous events, competing critical cues, stage palette, overlap footprint and resolution when cues conflict.

Safety and accessibility

Fill in: Full recorded-sequence flash testing method/result; reduced motion/flash effects; colour alternatives; preserved gameplay information. No numeric pass is treated as a medical guarantee.

Performance

Fill in: Target devices/graphics levels; observed frame time and frame-time spikes; transparent coverage; active/emitted particles; texture residency; lights; instancing/pool cleanup. Hardware and measurement method are required.

LOD and reduced effects variants

Fill in: Describe what remains at each project quality tier. Preserve truth, timing and threat boundaries before retaining sparks, smoke, bloom or light.

Review observations and fixes

Fill in: Moment; symptom; evidence/capture; concrete parameter or phase change; expected result; priority; retest outcome. Change a stated cause, not merely “more polish.”

Evidence and release status

Fill in: Source IDs and claim IDs; evidence level per claim; inferred values and test results; unresolved gaps; owner/version/date; pass/fail against the required checks.

Machine card template

effect_card_template.json in the package holds explicit nulls for unchosen numeric values, frame-rate context and evidence references. Null means not established; it must never be silently converted to zero or a production default.

09 Review checklist

Block in the primary shapes and timing before polishing. The requested four-part repair order separates communication/importance from visibility for review convenience; it is not presented as Riot’s verbatim list. Safety and performance are release gates throughout.

Ranked fix order

Truth: correct actionable area and timing.
Communication: identity, consequence, magnitude and importance.
Visibility: shape, value, clutter and background compatibility.
Theme and polish after prior gates pass.

Pass and fail review


1 Write the communication job and viewers

pass: Identity, consequence, magnitude, audience and timing authority are explicit.
if failed: Resolve missing gameplay facts before polishing.
evidence: inference; ES-S03

2 Block in with available simple parts

pass: Primary silhouette and temporal sequence read without rich textures or glow.
if failed: Swap to coarse library assets/meshes and retime the core.
evidence: industry practice; ES-S09, ES-S10

3 Check truth first

pass: Authoritative area, contact and active interval are accurately represented in every variant.
if failed: Fix semantic geometry/timing before hierarchy or theme.
evidence: industry practice; ES-S01

4 Check importance and meaning

pass: Viewers identify the effect and choose the intended response relative to competing cues.
if failed: Change focal region or viewer-specific priority.
evidence: industry practice; test inference; ES-S02, ES-S03

5 Frame step each phase

pass: No accidental pop, reversal, mismatched hit or misleading final active frame.
if failed: Adjust one responsible parameter/layer, then replay at normal speed.
evidence: industry practice; test inference; ES-S18, ES-S09

6 Inspect slow playback and timing curves

pass: Windup, punch/crescendo, follow-through and dissipation have deliberate transitions.
if failed: Retune the core phase; avoid assuming slow playback itself proves good feel.
evidence: industry practice; test inference; ES-S07, ES-S11

7 Inspect grayscale silhouette and squint small view

pass: Actionable geometry and primary form survive loss of hue/detail.
if failed: Repair value/shape separation; keep colour semantics redundantly encoded.
evidence: inference; ES-S10, ES-S02

8 Test actual phone size and graphics quality

pass: Recognition and required cues survive intended device, distance and reduced-polish conditions.
if failed: Use a simpler variant and repeat performance/accessibility review.
evidence: inference; 

9 Test bright dark and busy stages

pass: No permitted background or camera angle erases the primary message.
if failed: Adjust stage support or contrast treatment.
evidence: industry practice; ES-S02, ES-S17

10 Test the crowded scene

pass: Targets, path, pickups and essential UI remain understandable during credible overlaps.
if failed: Trim irrelevant audiences, ornamental layers, residue or simultaneous onsets.
evidence: inference; ES-S15, ES-S22

11 Test with sound on and off

pass: Picture communicates its required meaning alone; audiovisual peak does not contradict contact.
if failed: Separate visual/readability failure from sound-sync failure.
evidence: inference; 

12 Review comfort and safety jointly with other effects

pass: Required accessibility checks and reduced-effect settings pass; camera control remains usable.
if failed: Block release for unresolved safety/accessibility failures.
evidence: inference; safety criteria supplied by Output 3 safety and synchrony section; 

13 Polish theme only after communication passes

pass: Theme enhances the same meaning and does not recreate clutter or ambiguity.
if failed: Revert polish that regresses earlier checks.
evidence: industry practice; ES-S01

14 Record a reproducible comparison

pass: Before/after share gameplay seed, camera and competing effects, with precise measurements.
if failed: Capture comparable evidence and state uncertainty.
evidence: inference; ES-S23

15 A warning is readable without flipbook motion post effects

pass: Critical area, timing and identity still communicated in fallback
if failed: Correct the specified failure and rerun the affected scene and device cases.
evidence: inference; RB02, RB15, RB24

16 The sheet does not skip its meaningful onset

pass: First meaningful/contact frame aligns with timeline, including empty cells and random-start policy
if failed: Correct the specified failure and rerun the affected scene and device cases.
evidence: inference; RB04

17 Every cosmetic layer has a role

pass: Removing a layer has a named perceptual cost; no redundant duplicate smoke/glow
if failed: Correct the specified failure and rerun the affected scene and device cases.
evidence: inference informed by industry practice; RB38

18 Performance survives concurrency and sustained play

pass: Project-agreed frame/memory envelope met on baseline device through 10–15-minute active test
if failed: Correct the specified failure and rerun the affected scene and device cases.
evidence: spec guidance + inference acceptance; RB30

19 The effect ends and can be interrupted

pass: No frozen particles, old trails, lights, highlights, callbacks or camera offsets survive cleanup
if failed: Correct the specified failure and rerun the affected scene and device cases.
evidence: inference; RB01, RB06, RB08, RB23

20 Composite flash and reduced motion review

pass: Machine safety preflight passes the selected standard/version and tested footage; critical state remains readable with optional shake, blur and flash reduced.
if failed: Redesign failure before participant exposure; settings and warnings alone do not fix hazardous output.
evidence: industry practice and test inference; SA01, SA02, SA03, SA04

10 Genre presets

These eight profiles are proposed emphases for project testing. They do not prescribe universal particle counts, colours, timings or shake values.

Simulator

profile: Routine collection and conversion should read cheaply and clearly; reserve contrast for meaningful capacity, unlock and milestone transitions.
priorities: Pickup/counter convergence and explicit state confirmation.
main risk: Many repeated pickups and nearby players; combine low-importance feedback and keep a stable current balance.
application: Avoid max-tier reward spectacle on every click; test repetition and motivation instead of assuming escalation helps.
evidence level: inference: proposed project profile, not validated genre-wide numeric defaults

Destruction

profile: Structural change is the primary event; sell mass with large pieces, cause-following secondary breaks and material response.
priorities: Fracture location, moving mass, new openings and residual hazards.
main risk: Dust and overlapping debris can hide traversal; preserve escape routes and surviving targets.
application: Spend on readable silhouette and staged fragments before fine particles. Profile crowded collapses and cleanup.
evidence level: inference: proposed project profile, not validated genre-wide numeric defaults

Battlegrounds and combat

profile: Threat, hit confirmation and opponent state outrank theme.
priorities: Truthful telegraph, trackable projectile, contact result, owner/team distinction.
main risk: Many players and skins; reduce unrelated cosmetic layers while preserving opponent threat information.
application: Keep attack cadence and input readability intact. Critical/final feedback must not hide the next live threat.
evidence level: inference: proposed project profile, not validated genre-wide numeric defaults

Horror

profile: Use absence, contrast and restrained motion to support uncertainty without obscuring required information.
priorities: Source-local atmosphere, readable danger state, sparse anomalies.
main risk: Dark environments can make every emissive fleck dominant; fog may hide navigation.
application: Use atmosphere outside decision-critical areas. Avoid repetitive flashes and forced disorienting camera effects.
evidence level: inference: proposed project profile, not validated genre-wide numeric defaults

Obby

profile: Navigation and platform boundaries lead; movement VFX support timing and destination.
priorities: Takeoff, landing, dash destination, checkpoints and failure states.
main risk: Speed lines, bloom and trails can cover platform edges.
application: Maintain stable camera and clear path in reduced motion. Do not let decorative trails imply traversable geometry.
evidence level: inference: proposed project profile, not validated genre-wide numeric defaults

Tycoon

profile: Build-state change and resource flow should be immediately attributable to a cause.
priorities: Placement confirmation, completed machine, resource transfer and unlock.
main risk: Dense machines plus counters create competing motion and constant loops.
application: Keep ambient machine effects subordinate and local; milestone VFX ends in a stable completed state.
evidence level: inference: proposed project profile, not validated genre-wide numeric defaults

Disaster survival

profile: The current lethal hazard and safe route have priority over spectacle.
priorities: Truthful hazard boundary/state, directional threat, structural change and navigation.
main risk: Large weather, collapse and multiplayer effects coincide.
application: Degrade cosmetic smoke/debris before threat geometry. Test the worst overlap at low quality and on phones.
evidence level: inference: proposed project profile, not validated genre-wide numeric defaults

Anime style

profile: Use graphic silhouettes, directional accents and cadence contrast inside a coherent combat vocabulary.
priorities: Readable attack preparation, distinct impact, held graphic shape and designed breakup.
main risk: Impact frames, speed lines and saturated effects can stack into an unreadable flash field.
application: Treat stepped cadence and high contrast as contextual style choices. Do not assume cinematic inversion flashes are safe or gameplay-readable.
evidence level: inference: proposed project profile, not validated genre-wide numeric defaults

11 Glossary

Definitions use established field terms. Cadence requires an explicit base frame rate; a frame count alone is not a duration. Engine property names remain distinct from perceptual quantities.
Gameplay: The information and decisions the effect must support, including identity, action and consequence.
Shape: The silhouette and arrangement of masses that make an effect recognizable.
Value: The light-to-dark structure, independent of hue.
Colour: Hue, saturation and their relationships within the effect and scene.
Timing: How visual change is distributed through the effect’s life and aligned to events.
Composition: Arrangement and hierarchy that directs attention within an effect and across the scene.
Windup: The preparatory phase before the main action; often anticipation.
Anticipation: Preparation that makes the following action expected and legible.
Punch: The concentrated high-intensity accent of the action or contact.
Crescendo: A build in intensity toward a peak; it need not appear in every effect.
Follow-through: Motion that continues after the principal action as energy transfers and resolves.
Dissipation: The designed ending in which the effect disperses or loses prominence.
Slow in and slow out: Acceleration and deceleration that make timing nonuniform.
Squash and stretch: Changing proportion to communicate deformation, motion or force while preserving intended volume impression.
Arc: A curved motion path used to organize gesture or flow.
Overlap: Related components move or settle at different times rather than as one rigid unit.
Silhouette: The recognizable outer shape, assessable without texture detail.
Line of action: The dominant directional gesture of an effect or movement.
Primary shape: The dominant mass or gesture carrying the effect’s essential meaning.
Secondary element: A supporting component that strengthens the primary action without displacing it.
Tertiary detail: Fine supporting ornament; usually a candidate for reduction before primary information.
Breakup: Fragmenting a solid shape or texture into irregular pieces.
Erosion: Progressive removal of a shape, often through a mask, rather than uniform transparency.
Dissolve: A spatially varying disappearance driven by a pattern or threshold.
Bloom: A post effect that spreads bright areas into surrounding pixels; it is not geometry or a damage boundary.
Emissive: An appearance of self-illumination; in Roblox light emission alone does not mean light cast onto the scene.
Additive blending: Combining light contributions by addition, tending to brighten overlapping regions.
Alpha blending: Combining foreground and background using transparency; ordering and overlap matter.
Flipbook: A sequence of images stored in a sheet or atlas and played as animation.
Sprite sheet: An image atlas containing individual frames or sprites.
One-shot: An animation intended to play through once per event.
Loop: Animation that repeats; its end-to-start transition needs design.
On ones: A new drawing or pose on each frame of the stated base timebase.
On twos: A drawing or pose held for two frames of the stated base timebase; not inherently 2 fps.
Variable cadence: Changing the number of held base frames between image updates.
Impact frame: A brief graphic accent at impact, which may change silhouette, colour or contrast.
Hit-stop: A brief pause or hold associated with contact; clarify whether simulation, animation or only presentation stops.
Freeze frame: A held image or pose; it may be cinematic rather than a gameplay-wide pause.
Camera kick: A directional camera displacement or rotation linked to an event.
Screen shake: Time-varying camera or screen movement used to reinforce an event.
Trauma: In Eiserloh’s camera model, a state variable accumulated by events and decayed over time to drive shake nonlinearly.
Telegraph: A cue announcing an action or hazard before activation.
Hitbox: The gameplay geometry used to determine contact or damage; its visual indicator must represent it truthfully.
Salience: How strongly an item attracts attention relative to its context.
Crowding: Impaired identification of a target because nearby visual elements interfere, especially in peripheral vision.
Clutter: Visual competition that makes relevant information harder to locate or identify.
Overdraw: Repeated shading of overlapping pixels; broad transparent layers can make cost high.
LOD: Level of detail; a project’s method for reducing presentation cost while preserving essential information.
Culling: Avoiding rendering or updating content that is not needed under defined visibility or relevance conditions.
Pooling: Reusing instances rather than repeatedly creating and destroying them; requires reliable reset and cleanup.
Billboard: A flat element oriented toward the camera or another defined direction.
Depth cue: Information that helps communicate distance, layering or spatial relationships.
Attachment: A Roblox local reference frame used to place or connect components.
Beam: A Roblox connection rendered between attachments, useful for continuous paths and arcs.
Trail: A Roblox strip generated from attachment movement over time.
ZOffset: A ParticleEmitter rendering-depth offset; it does not move gameplay geometry.
TimeScale: A ParticleEmitter control affecting particle simulation speed, separate from global gameplay time.
Harding test: Common shorthand for automated photosensitive-epilepsy flash/pattern analysis; tool, version and recorded sequence must be specified.
Kitbashing: Combining and adapting existing parts into a new effect rather than authoring every component from scratch.
Block-in: Testing the main shapes, motion and timing before texture/detail polish.
fill rate: Capacity to process screen pixels; a few large sprites can cost more than many tiny ones.
alpha/normal blending: Compositing that preserves occluding color according to opacity.
mip: A lower-resolution texture representation used at smaller projected sizes or under resource constraints.
OneShot: Roblox flipbook mode that fits a complete cell sequence across the particle lifetime.
on 2s: A drawing held for two frames of a stated presentation frame rate; not a universal update frequency.

12 Gaps

Missing numerical evidence is a result, not permission to fabricate a default. These targeted tests would convert uncertainty into project-specific design data.

Universal phase timings

what remains unknown: No validated light/heavy/reward phase-duration table transfers across genres, cameras and input cadences.
how to test: Compare timing variants while holding asset art and sound fixed. Measure contact identification, response performance, perceived weight, preference and fatigue. Store display fps, capture fps, game timebase and actual ms.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Importance to parameter mapping

what remains unknown: Riot’s importance scale does not publish a universal mapping to size, luminance, duration or layer count.
how to test: Establish ranked simultaneous-cue tasks; vary one prominence channel at a time; test whether participants identify the most consequential event correctly.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Screen shake and hit stop

what remains unknown: Named examples and models are not safe default amplitudes, frequencies or durations for Roblox.
how to test: Test device/camera-specific variants with optional controls; measure aim/navigation errors, comfort and hit identification alongside perceived impact. Keep gameplay freeze distinct from animation-only hold.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Flash timing and area

what remains unknown: A legal or technical threshold is not an artistic target or guarantee of medical safety.
how to test: Analyze full-screen recordings of overlapping effects at worst viewing conditions; record test method/version and results. Test reduced-flash variants and seek specialist review when risk remains.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Simultaneous effect limit

what remains unknown: No universal maximum count or screen percentage establishes readability across effects.
how to test: Stress the intended busiest scene; vary transparent footprint, overlap and importance distribution; measure target identification, hazard avoidance and frame-time percentiles.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Mobile budgets

what remains unknown: No device-independent particle, light, layer, texture-residency or frame-time budget is established.
how to test: Profile representative low-end devices and actual graphics settings. Capture worst overlaps and long sessions; derive project budgets from measured bottlenecks.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Genre and reward transfer

what remains unknown: The cited juice studies are not direct validation for simulator monetization loops or a common-to-legendary reveal ladder.
how to test: Compare clear restrained feedback with alternatives using comprehension, enjoyment and repeated-session measures. Do not infer player welfare or long-term retention from a short experiment.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Repetition and adaptation

what remains unknown: No validated variant count, randomization range, cooldown, combo step size or reset duration transfers universally.
how to test: Use repeated exposure with semantic invariants held fixed. Track recognition, fatigue, perceived consistency and task interference; test aggregation and attenuation as separate interventions.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Audiovisual synchrony

what remains unknown: Psychophysical detection windows are task- and stimulus-dependent, not a plug-in latency budget.
how to test: Measure actual display/audio onset together on target devices; assess detection and impact under realistic input/network timing. Compare offsets without altering sound identity or visual intensity.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Shape and hue meaning

what remains unknown: Simple emotion labels for circles, triangles or hues are not universal causal laws.
how to test: Test the project vocabulary with unfamiliar players and accessibility modes; distinguish learned convention from direct recognition and cultural association.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Flipbook resolution in runtime

what remains unknown: Upload size does not guarantee runtime resident size or effective visible resolution for every asset path.
how to test: Inspect actual particle appearance and available memory measurements on target devices; compare cell sizes and projected size, including compression, edges and mip behavior.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Variable artistic cadence

what remains unknown: Film on-twos/on-sixes practice does not establish a Roblox implementation or gameplay benefit.
how to test: Compare duplicated atlas frames, external sequence control and smooth playback for the same asset; measure tracking and silhouette readability. Preserve authoritative gameplay timing.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Source breadth

what remains unknown: Some requested candidate titles lack publicly read, maker-attributed breakdowns. Abstracts, portfolios and fan footage cannot substitute for detailed production evidence.
how to test: Prioritize direct creator interviews/talk recordings for anime, Roblox exemplars and underrepresented juicy games. Add only claims actually documented in accessible material.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Long term experience

what remains unknown: Available short-term or correlational results cannot establish thousands-of-plays comfort, accessibility, retention or spending effects.
how to test: Run longitudinal, consented tests with stable gameplay and participant-controlled effects; predefine outcomes and report attrition rather than selecting favorable metrics.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Scene palette and salience

what remains unknown: Laboratory attention and crowding findings do not directly prescribe a game’s luminance or saturation ratios.
how to test: Use realistic scenes with competing tasks, alternative palettes and multiple camera distances; measure detection and false positives, then document the project-specific range.
evidence level: inference: proposed validation plan

Field coverage

what remains unknown: Roblox: two official worked examples found, but no sufficient first-hand detailed production breakdowns for Blox Fruits, DOORS or Pet Simulator 99. Fan guesses and asset recreations were not promoted to studio evidence.
how to test: Seek a maker-attributed breakdown, inspect the full source and verify the claimed method before use.
evidence level: research gap

Field coverage

what remains unknown: Stylized games: Hi-Fi RUSH and Balatro have useful maker testimony; Hades evidence here establishes intention more than emitter construction. Sparkball and Riot cases are covered by Outputs 1 and 3. Other famous games were excluded without usable documentation.
how to test: Seek a maker-attributed breakdown, inspect the full source and verify the claimed method before use.
evidence level: research gap

Field coverage

what remains unknown: Anime: three named-maker cases exist, but two are individual animator interviews rather than studio technical publications. No controlled evidence for a universally optimal impact-frame count or brightness was found.
how to test: Seek a maker-attributed breakdown, inspect the full source and verify the claimed method before use.
evidence level: research gap

Field coverage

what remains unknown: Rocksteady 2024 and Beyond-FX 2026 are abstract-only; their contents must not be represented as fully watched/read lectures.
how to test: Seek a maker-attributed breakdown, inspect the full source and verify the claimed method before use.
evidence level: research gap

Field coverage

what remains unknown: Rainbow Six 2016 is explicitly historical. Siege X 2025 description provides modern design context but no verification that old replication/collision details persist.
how to test: Seek a maker-attributed breakdown, inspect the full source and verify the claimed method before use.
evidence level: research gap

Field coverage

what remains unknown: LEGO Fortnite official Chaos talk exists, but only its description was inspected; it is a lead, not detailed evidence. Do not assert its fracture solver or toy-brick VFX recipe.
how to test: Seek a maker-attributed breakdown, inspect the full source and verify the claimed method before use.
evidence level: research gap

Field coverage

what remains unknown: Teardown reverse-engineering blogs were excluded from first-hand implementation claims; developer design sources are stronger for player consequence than for exact modern renderer internals.
how to test: Seek a maker-attributed breakdown, inspect the full source and verify the claimed method before use.
evidence level: research gap

Field coverage

what remains unknown: No inspected field source validates universal light/medium/heavy VFX timings, dust lifetimes, debris counts, luminosity ratios, camera-shake amplitudes or flash frequencies.
how to test: Seek a maker-attributed breakdown, inspect the full source and verify the claimed method before use.
evidence level: research gap

Field coverage

what remains unknown: Film techniques were executed with controlled cameras and offline resources. A Roblox kitbash reproduces selected visual cues only, unless separate gameplay/simulation systems provide the physical consequence.
how to test: Seek a maker-attributed breakdown, inspect the full source and verify the claimed method before use.
evidence level: research gap

Field coverage

what remains unknown: Correct talk metadata: Controlled Chaos: 12 Principles of Design for VFX is Rachel Quitevis / Beyond-FX, GDC 2026. Hanno Hinkelbein / Rocksteady, GDC 2024 is Attention Overload: Creating Readable VFX.
how to test: Seek a maker-attributed breakdown, inspect the full source and verify the claimed method before use.
evidence level: research gap

Evidence contradictions and limits


AUD 01

Finding: Figure 4 gives curiosity→playtime .88 [.42,1.35] in Model A; §4.2 text says .99. Table 2 labels overall playtime mean 13.86, SD 7.90; §5.3 calls 7.9 the mean and reports 10.8%. Suppress that percentage pending author/code verification.
Evidence: inference (direct internal-consistency audit); JS01

AUD 02

Finding: These are different experimental operationalisations, not a single dose-response curve overturned by the newer paper. Neither establishes an optimum for Roblox children, phones, multiplayer or extended sessions.
Evidence: inference (cross-study scope comparison); JS01, JS02

AUD 03

Finding: Performance measures include accumulated actions/kills/level while playtime differs. Do not translate them into improved per-minute skill or accuracy. Expert-designed None was a condition name, not proof of literally absent feedback.
Evidence: inference (measurement audit); JS02

AUD 04

Finding: Keep arXiv version labelled preprint, while acknowledging later IEEE GEM publication. Feature presence in selected commercial games is observational; no universal necessity theorem follows. Frame examples are authors’ descriptions, not a validated prescription.
Evidence: inference (publication and method audit); JS03

AUD 05

Finding: The 2025 arXiv posting is an ICMI 2024 author manuscript. Some surrounding results prose conflicts with tables (e.g. mastery direction, duplicated challenge means). Use the internally consistent progress-feedback result, not the contradictory passages.
Evidence: inference (metadata and text audit); JS04

AUD 06

Finding: Microsoft’s approximate 20%-screen wording and older red formula are not interchangeable with WCAG visual-field geometry and updated red criterion. Record tool, standard and version; never merge them into an invented threshold.
Evidence: inference (standards comparison); SA01, SA02, SA03

AUD 07

Finding: The 2017 League guide discourages extreme saturation/value; Sparkball’s 2023 maker account reports that faint desaturated effects failed its busy scene and stronger crisp shapes worked. Context changed; do not turn either project’s palette into a universal rule.
Evidence: inference from differing production contexts; ES-S05, ES-S07

AUD 08

Finding: Current general texture guidance permits 4096 by 4096 uploads while an older UV subsection still says 1024 by 1024. Upload maximum does not establish runtime particle resolution.
Evidence: spec comparison; RB26, RB27

AUD 09

Finding: The ColorGradingEffect class specifies Lighting-only parenting, overriding the broad post-effects tutorial implication that all such effects may use Camera.
Evidence: spec comparison; RB21, RB33

AUD 10

Finding: The requested 1–10 importance scale is a reported League exercise with a single exact numerical source; broader official clarity guidance corroborates hierarchy, not the exact scale or any parameter mapping.
Evidence: industry practice with provenance limitation; ES-S03, ES-S02

Source register

Sources were read within the access scope stated here. A catalog abstract supports a talk’s title, speaker and stated scope only. Source tiers describe provenance, while evidence levels describe the kind of claim. Different IDs may resolve to the same publication when it supports separate research sections; aliases are recorded in the package.
